children.title: Relaxation-Numerics Failure Family
children.top_down_role: Failure modes producing weak, invalid, or nonrigorous global bounds.

children.title: Formulation-Sensitive Relaxation Weakness
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for large gaps and representation-dependent relaxation strength.

children.title: Weak Relaxation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem structures producing persistently large relaxation gaps.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous Families with Unbounded Relaxation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary continuous examples showing that both weak-family regimes can occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For additive weakness, let \(P_n\) minimize \(x\) subject to \(x^2=0\) and \(-n\le x\le0\). Its optimum is \(v_n=0\). Dropping \(x^2=0\) gives the valid continuous relaxation \(-n\le x\le0\) with value \(r_n=-n\), hence \(v_n-r_n=n\). For multiplicative weakness, let \(Q_n\) minimize \(x\) subject to \(x=1\) and \(1/n\le x\le1\). Dropping \(x=1\) gives the valid continuous relaxation \(1/n\le x\le1\), with exact value \(v_n=1\), relaxation value \(r_n=1/n\), and ratio \(v_n/r_n=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple continuous problem families obtained by dropping an equality have additive gaps or positive optimum-to-bound ratios growing like n.
assumptions_latex: Each relaxation is formed by deleting the displayed equality while retaining its bounding interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v_n-r_n=n\to+\infty\quad\text{and}\quad \frac{v_n}{r_n}=n\to+\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Families with Unbounded Relaxation Gaps

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additive and Multiplicative Weak Relaxation Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convention-explicit family-level definitions of unbounded relaxation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_i\) be minimization problems with finite optima \(v_i\), and let \(r_i\le v_i\) be values of valid relaxations. The family is additively weak when \[\sup_i(v_i-r_i)=+\infty.\] If additionally \(0<r_i\le v_i\) for every \(i\), it is multiplicatively weak when \[\sup_i\frac{v_i}{r_i}=+\infty.\] Additive weakness is invariant under a common translation of each objective and scales with positive objective rescaling. Multiplicative weakness is invariant under positive rescaling but not under objective translation, so it is meaningful only under the stated positive-value convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation family is additively weak when its absolute value gaps are unbounded, and multiplicatively weak when positive optimum-to-bound ratios are unbounded. Ratio weakness is not translation-invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_i(v_i-r_i)=+\infty\Rightarrow\text{no uniform finite additive guarantee},\quad \sup_i(v_i/r_i)=+\infty\Rightarrow\text{no uniform finite multiplicative guarantee}.

notation.meaning: valid relaxation value for problem i

knowledge_statements.title: Additive and Multiplicative Weak Relaxation Families
Weak Relaxation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative regime where relaxation bounds fail to approximate the original optimum uniformly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimization problems \(P_n\) with finite optima \(v_n\) and relaxations \(R_n\) having lower-bound values \(r_n\le v_n\). The family is in an additively weak relaxation regime when \(v_n-r_n\) is unbounded as \(n\to\infty\). For problems with \(0<r_n\le v_n\), it is multiplicatively weak when \(v_n/r_n\) is unbounded. Consequently, no constant independent of \(n\) can bound the corresponding additive or multiplicative relaxation error throughout the family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation regime is weak when its additive or multiplicative optimal-value gap becomes arbitrarily large across a problem family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No uniform finite additive, respectively multiplicative, approximation guarantee follows from the relaxation values.

notation.meaning: optimal value of the original problem
optimal value of its minimization relaxation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unbounded integrality or relaxation gaps are the standard quantitative signature of relaxation weakness
source treating continuous global-optimization relaxation-gap families is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf and the formulas are plausible, but a source is required for this continuous global-optimization use of additive and multiplicative relaxation weakness. “Unbounded as n approaches infinity” should also be fixed as a precise supremum or limsup condition.

children.title: Formulation-Sensitive Relaxation Strength
children.top_down_role: Variation in relaxation quality across mathematically equivalent formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Formulation-Sensitive Relaxation Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation bounds can differ across equivalent formulations of the same feasible optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let formulations \(P^1\) and \(P^2\) project onto the same feasible set in the original variable \(x\) and have the same objective \(f(x)\), hence the same optimum \(v\). Let their minimization relaxations have values \(r_1\) and \(r_2\). Relaxation strength is formulation-sensitive whenever \(r_1\ne r_2\); formulation \(1\) is at least as strong as formulation \(2\) when \(r_1\ge r_2\), and strictly stronger when \(r_1>r_2\). Thus equivalence of exact feasible projections does not imply equality of relaxation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent exact formulations may produce different relaxation bounds; for minimization, the formulation with the larger valid lower bound is stronger.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_1>r_2\) implies that formulation \(1\) has the strictly tighter relaxation bound for the common minimization problem.

notation.meaning: extended feasible set of formulation j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: minimization relaxations are ordered by their valid lower-bound values
source exhibiting formulation-dependent relaxation strength in continuous global optimization is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the leaf, but no source supports the exact formulation-dependent claim. Comparing only r_1 and r_2 defines objective-specific bound strength; the broader term “relaxation strength” often denotes feasible-region containment or dominance across objectives, so the intended notion needs sourced qualification.

children.title: Equivalent-Representation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Bound-quality differences induced by alternate expression or lifting choices.

assumptions_latex: Interval operations are evaluated by the natural interval extension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_1(X)=[-1,1]\neq[0,1]=F_2(X)\), although both expressions have exact range \([0,1/4]\).

notation.meaning: Natural interval extensions of the two expressions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete gap between natural interval extensions of algebraically equivalent expressions.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1(x)=x-x^2\) and \(f_2(x)=x(1-x)\). These expressions define the same real function on \(X=[0,1]\). Their natural interval extensions satisfy \[F_1(X)=X-X^2=[-1,1],\qquad F_2(X)=X(1-X)=[0,1].\] The exact range of either expression is \(f_i(X)=[0,1/4]\). Thus algebraically equivalent representations can produce unequal relaxation enclosures and unequal lower bounds without changing the underlying optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent algebraic formulas can yield different interval relaxations: on [0,1], x-x² gives [-1,1], while x(1-x) gives [0,1], although both have exact range [0,1/4].
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent-Representation Gaps

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

children.title: Relaxation Weakness Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Structural indicators used to locate sources of poor relaxation quality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Certification Width and Formulation Spread Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rigorous absolute diagnostics for equivalent minimization formulations evaluated with a common incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For equivalent minimization formulations with common optimum \(f^*\), let \(L_j\le f^*\) be certified relaxation lower bounds and let \(U\ge f^*\) be the objective value of one common feasible incumbent. Define \(W_j:=U-L_j\) and \(S:=\max_jL_j-\min_jL_j\). Then \(0\le f^*-L_j\le W_j\) and \(0\le U-f^*\le W_j\). Moreover, \(S>0\) certifies that the tested equivalent formulations produce different relaxation bounds for the common objective. These quantities are absolute diagnostics; declaring them large requires a stated tolerance or objective scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common incumbent minus a certified lower bound is a rigorous certification width, while the spread of lower bounds detects formulation-sensitive bound differences. Interpreting either as large requires a declared scale.
assumptions_latex: All formulations have the same feasible objective values and finite common optimum \(f^*\).
Each \(L_j\) is a certified lower bound.
\(U\) is the value of a feasible point shared by the exact problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\le f^*-L_j\le W_j,\quad 0\le U-f^*\le W_j,\quad S>0\Rightarrow\exists i,j:\ L_i\ne L_j.

notation.meaning: certified relaxation lower bound for formulation j
absolute certification width for formulation j

knowledge_statements.title: Certification Width and Formulation Spread Diagnostics

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prevents certification width from being misidentified as relaxation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A large certification width \(U-L_j\) does not by itself show that relaxation \(j\) is weak: the width decomposes as \[(U-f^*)+(f^*-L_j),\] so it may be caused by incumbent suboptimality, relaxation error, or both. Likewise, a zero formulation spread shows only that the tested formulations return equal lower bounds; it does not certify that their common bound is tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large incumbent-to-bound gap does not isolate relaxation weakness, and equal bounds across formulations do not imply tightness.
assumptions_latex: The compared formulations have a common exact optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U-L_j\text{ alone does not identify }f^*-L_j,\qquad S=0\not\Rightarrow L_j=f^*.
knowledge_statements.title: Gap Attribution Boundary

assumptions_latex: Each formulation \(P_j\) has the same feasible objective values and a valid relaxation lower bound \(L_j\).
A common feasible incumbent supplies an upper bound \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Large values of \(G_j=U-L_j\) diagnose weak relaxations, while large \(S=\max_jL_j-\min_jL_j\) diagnose formulation sensitivity.

notation.meaning: Valid relaxation lower bound for formulation j.
Objective value of a common feasible incumbent.

review_flags: Exact diagnostic conventions require a dedicated relaxation reference.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound-gap diagnostics for equivalent minimization formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For equivalent minimization formulations \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\), let each relaxation return a certified lower bound \(L_j\le f^*\), and let \(U\ge f^*\) be the value of a feasible incumbent. Define the absolute relaxation gap \(G_j=U-L_j\) and the formulation spread \[S=\max_{1\le j\le m}L_j-\min_{1\le j\le m}L_j.\] A large \(G_j\) relative to the chosen objective scale diagnoses weak pruning power. A large \(S\) diagnoses representation sensitivity because equivalent feasible objective sets are producing materially different relaxation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare each valid lower bound with a common incumbent and compare bounds across equivalent formulations. Large gaps indicate weakness; a large cross-formulation spread indicates representation sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Weakness Diagnostics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gap and spread are plausible diagnostic quantities, but no source supports these conventions, and the meaning of a large value depends on an unspecified objective scale or threshold.

children.title: Interval Overestimation Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for interval overestimation from repeated variables and enclosure geometry.

children.title: Interval Dependency
children.top_down_role: Overestimation caused by lost dependence between repeated expression occurrences.

assumptions_latex: Each occurrence of a variable is evaluated independently by natural interval arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The natural interval extension gives \(X-X=[-2,2]\), whereas the exact range of \(x-x\) is \(\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical dependency overestimation in natural interval arithmetic.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the real expression \(f(x)=x-x\) on \(X=[-1,1]\), the two occurrences of \(x\) represent the same value, so the exact range is \(f(X)=\{0\}\). Natural interval evaluation loses this dependence and computes \[F(X)=X-X=[-1,1]-[-1,1]=[-2,2].\] Hence inclusion monotonicity preserves containment, but repeated independent use of the same interval can create strict overestimation even when the represented function is constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Natural interval arithmetic treats repeated occurrences independently: x-x on [-1,1] encloses to [-2,2], although its exact range is the singleton zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval Dependency

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

children.title: Wrapping Overestimation
children.top_down_role: Enclosure growth caused by repeatedly enclosing transformed sets in simple regions.

assumptions_latex: Every intermediate set is replaced by its axis-aligned interval hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Two exact inverse rotations represented through interval hulls expand \(B\) to \([-2,2]^2\), although \(R^{\mathsf T}RB=B\).

notation.meaning: Rotation matrix through pi over four.
Smallest axis-aligned box containing a set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wrapping caused by repeated axis-aligned enclosure of transformed sets.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=[-1,1]^2\), let \(R\) rotate vectors through \(\pi/4\), and let \(\square(S)\) denote the smallest axis-aligned box containing \(S\). Exact propagation gives \(R^{\mathsf T}RB=B\). Interval-hull propagation instead gives \[\square(RB)=[-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}]^2,\qquad \square\!\left(R^{\mathsf T}\square(RB)\right)=[-2,2]^2.\] The enlargement occurs solely because correlation and orientation are discarded after the intermediate rotation; repeated propagation can compound this wrapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box rotated 45 degrees, boxed, and rotated back expands from [-1,1]² to [-2,2]², although the exact composed transformation is the identity.
knowledge_statements.title: Wrapping Overestimation

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Width comparison between sequential axis-aligned enclosure and direct enclosure of composed linear maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subset\mathbb R^n\) be an axis-aligned box with width vector \(w\ge0\), and let \(A,C\) be compatible real matrices. Then \(\operatorname{wid}(\square(AB))=|A|w\), so sequential enclosure has width \(|C||A|w\), whereas direct enclosure under the composition has width \(|CA|w\). Consequently, \[|CA|w\le |C||A|w\] componentwise. A strict component records wrapping introduced solely by the intermediate box hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequentially boxing linear images gives width |C||A|w, never smaller than the direct composed-image width |CA|w; strict inequality is wrapping loss.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is an axis-aligned box with finite width vector \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{wid}(\square(C\square(AB)))=|C||A|w\ge |CA|w=\operatorname{wid}(\square(CAB))\) componentwise.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Box-Wrapping Inequality

children.title: Repeated-Variable Effects
children.top_down_role: Expression structures where multiple occurrences of a variable weaken interval ranges.

assumptions_latex: Division uses the standard interval quotient because \(0\notin X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The natural interval quotient is \(X/X=[1/2,2]\), while the exact range of \(x/x\) is \(\{1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated-variable loss of correlation in interval division.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=x/x\) on \(X=[1,2]\). Since numerator and denominator are the same nonzero real number, \(f(x)=1\) and the exact range is \(f(X)=\{1\}\). Evaluating the two occurrences independently gives \[F(X)=X/X=[1,2]\,[1/2,1]=[1/2,2].\] Thus repeated-variable occurrence can introduce overestimation even when every elementary operation is defined and the final function is constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For x in [1,2], x/x is exactly 1, but independent interval evaluation of the repeated variable produces [1/2,2].
knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Variable Effects

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

children.title: Enclosure-Geometry Effects
children.top_down_role: Interaction between enclosure shape and the geometry of propagated sets.

assumptions_latex: Enclosures are restricted to axis-aligned boxes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The area ratio between the interval hull and the represented set equals \((1+\varepsilon)^2/(2\varepsilon)\), which diverges as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: Rotation matrix through pi over four.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded relative overestimation for thin, obliquely oriented sets.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), define the rotated rectangle \[S_\varepsilon=R\{(u,v):|u|\le1,\ |v|\le\varepsilon\},\] where \(R\) rotates through \(\pi/4\). Its area is \(4\varepsilon\), whereas its axis-aligned interval hull is \(\square(S_\varepsilon)=[-(1+\varepsilon)/\sqrt{2},(1+\varepsilon)/\sqrt{2}]^2\), with area \(2(1+\varepsilon)^2\). Therefore the enclosure-to-set area ratio is \((1+\varepsilon)^2/(2\varepsilon)\), which tends to infinity as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Axis-aligned boxes can represent thin rotated sets arbitrarily poorly: the enclosure-to-set area ratio diverges as the rectangle becomes thinner.
knowledge_statements.title: Enclosure-Geometry Effects

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

children.title: Curvature-Bound Reliability Failures
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for degraded or invalid curvature-based bounds.

children.title: Scaling-Induced Bound Degradation
children.top_down_role: Loss of bound quality caused by poorly scaled variables, constraints, or objectives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaling Can Strictly Degrade a Gershgorin Curvature Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent diagonal variable scaling that turns a nonnegative Gershgorin curvature bound into a negative one and weakens the resulting alphaBB lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx\) on \(X=[-1,1]^2\), where \(H=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{pmatrix}\). The unscaled Gershgorin eigenvalue lower bound is \(1/2>0\), so no alphaBB curvature correction is required. Under \(x=Dy\) with \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1/4,1)\), the equivalent domain is \(Y=[-4,4]\times[-1,1]\) and the transformed Hessian is \(D^{\mathsf T}HD=\begin{pmatrix}1/16&1/8\\1/8&1\end{pmatrix}\), whose unscaled Gershgorin lower bound is \(-1/16\). Using the isotropic coefficient \(\alpha=1/32\) therefore adds a nonpositive separable box correction. At \(y=0\) that correction equals \(-17/32\), so the resulting lower model has minimum at most \(-17/32\), whereas the unscaled convex quadratic has exact minimum \(0\). Thus an equivalent variable scaling can strictly degrade a specified coordinatewise curvature relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagonal change of variables can make an unscaled Gershgorin curvature estimate negative even when the original estimate is positive, forcing an unnecessary alphaBB correction and a strictly weaker lower bound.
assumptions_latex: Curvature is bounded by the unscaled rowwise Gershgorin formula, and the isotropic alphaBB coefficient is \(\alpha=\max\{0,-\underline\lambda_G/2\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\underline\lambda_G(H)=\tfrac12,\quad \underline\lambda_G(D^{\mathsf T}HD)=-\tfrac1{16},\quad \min_Y q_\alpha\le-\tfrac{17}{32}<0=\min_X f.\)

notation.meaning: Unscaled Gershgorin lower bound on the smallest eigenvalue.
Transformed alphaBB lower model using the Gershgorin-derived correction.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Can Strictly Degrade a Gershgorin Curvature Relaxation

assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a nonsingular diagonal scaling matrix.
Curvature is estimated in the scaled coordinates \(x=Dy\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transformed Hessian is \(D^{\mathsf T}HD\), and its condition number may grow by a factor as large as \(\kappa_2(D)^2\).
review_flags: A dedicated source for scaling effects on global curvature relaxations is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate scaling can amplify conservative or inaccurate curvature estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the quadratic function \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx\) and the substitution \(x=Dy\), the Hessian becomes \(D^{\mathsf T}HD\). When \(H\) is positive definite, \[\kappa_2(D^{\mathsf T}HD)\le \kappa_2(D)^2\kappa_2(H),\] and families exist for which the dependence on \(\kappa_2(D)^2\) is attained. Thus an equivalent rescaling leaves the exact optimum unchanged but can substantially worsen conditioning and any relaxation bound obtained from coordinatewise or finite-precision curvature estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal rescaling preserves the exact optimization problem but can square the scaling condition number in the transformed Hessian, degrading curvature estimates and derived bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Induced Bound Degradation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hessian transformation and condition-number inequality are standard, but the record supplies no citation for the asserted connection to degradation of global curvature-relaxation bounds. Matrix dimensions should also be stated explicitly.

children.title: Curvature-Bound Invalidity
children.top_down_role: Cases where claimed curvature bounds do not rigorously cover the target region.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice differentiable on a convex set \(X\).
A claimed constant \(\widehat m\) is used as a lower bound for \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\) on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\widehat m>\inf_{x\in X}\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\), the resulting quadratic lower model need not be valid.

notation.meaning: Claimed uniform Hessian eigenvalue lower bound.
Reference point for the quadratic model.

review_flags: A dedicated source for curvature-certified underestimators is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a quadratic lower model under an invalid curvature bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic lower model based at \(x_0\in X\) is \[q(x)=f(x_0)+\nabla f(x_0)^{\mathsf T}(x-x_0)+\tfrac12\widehat m\|x-x_0\|_2^2.\] Its global validity requires \(\widehat m\le\inf_{x\in X}\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\). If this inequality fails, \(q\le f\) is not guaranteed. For example, with \(f(x)=-x^2\), \(X=[-1,1]\), \(x_0=0\), and \(\widehat m=0\), one obtains \(q(x)=0\), but \(q(1)=0>f(1)=-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curvature-based lower model can overestimate the objective if its claimed Hessian lower bound is too large; the concave quadratic -x² gives a direct counterexample.
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Bound Invalidity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly shows that an excessive curvature estimate can invalidate the lower model. However, the statement that the uniform eigenvalue inequality is required for validity of a particular fixed-base model is stronger than the supplied reasoning supports; the condition is a standard sufficient certificate, not generally a necessary condition for accidental pointwise validity.

children.title: Curvature-Estimate Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of relaxation strength on estimated curvature information.

assumptions_latex: Two separable quadratic underestimators differ only by curvature coefficients \(\alpha_i\) and \(\widetilde\alpha_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Their pointwise difference is at most \(\sum_i|\alpha_i-\widetilde\alpha_i|(u_i-l_i)^2/4\).
review_flags: A dedicated source for coefficient sensitivity of quadratic relaxations is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative sensitivity of separable quadratic relaxations to curvature estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[q_\alpha(x)=f(x)-\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i(x_i-l_i)(u_i-x_i)\] and define \(q_{\widetilde\alpha}\) analogously. Since \(0\le(x_i-l_i)(u_i-x_i)\le(u_i-l_i)^2/4\) on \(X\), \[|q_\alpha(x)-q_{\widetilde\alpha}(x)|\le\frac14\sum_{i=1}^n|\alpha_i-\widetilde\alpha_i|(u_i-l_i)^2.\] Consequently, the optimal lower bounds obtained by minimizing these two underestimators over the same feasible region differ by no more than the same quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbing a separable curvature coefficient changes the relaxation bound in proportion to the coefficient error and the square of that variable's interval width.
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Estimate Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise perturbation inequality is mathematically plausible, but no source is provided. The subsequent minimization claim refers to an undefined feasible region, and the statement includes derivational proof text rather than only the property.

children.title: Finite-Precision Curvature Effects
children.top_down_role: Loss of rigor or usefulness in curvature information under finite precision.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enclosure condition required for a floating-point interval-Hessian curvature certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(X)\) on a box \(X\), and let \(\boldsymbol H(X)\) be a computed interval matrix. A reported number \(\underline\lambda\) is a rigorous Hessian-eigenvalue lower bound if the computation certifies both \(\nabla^2f(x)\in\boldsymbol H(X)\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\ge\underline\lambda\) for every symmetric \(H\in\boldsymbol H(X)\). A finite-precision calculation lacking either enclosure establishes only an estimate, not a curvature certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-precision curvature bound is rigorous only when the interval Hessian encloses every true Hessian and the spectral lower bound is verified for every enclosed matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(\boldsymbol H(X)\) is intended to enclose the full Hessian range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl[\forall x\in X,\ \nabla^2f(x)\in\boldsymbol H(X)\bigr]\land\bigl[\forall H\in\boldsymbol H(X),\ \lambda_{\min}(H)\ge\underline\lambda\bigr]\Longrightarrow\forall x\in X,\ \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\ge\underline\lambda.\)

notation.meaning: Interval enclosure of the Hessian range on X.
Verified uniform lower bound on enclosed Hessian eigenvalues.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Curvature Certification Condition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearest Rounding Can Reverse a Curvature Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete loss of curvature-bound rigor when a negative Hessian entry is rounded upward.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a=-1-2^{-54}\) and \(f(x)=\tfrac12ax^2\) on \([-1,1]\). Suppose binary floating-point evaluation rounds \(a\) to nearest as \(\widehat a=-1\). Then the reported curvature lower bound \(\widehat a\) is nonconservative because \(f''(x)=a<\widehat a\). The quadratic model \(q(x)=\tfrac12\widehat a x^2\) therefore satisfies \(q(x)>f(x)\) for every \(x\ne0\), so it is not a valid lower model. Directed outward rounding to a representable value no greater than \(a\) avoids this particular failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounding a negative Hessian value upward can turn a purported curvature lower bound into an invalid one and make the resulting quadratic model exceed the objective.
assumptions_latex: The coefficient is rounded to nearest in a format for which it is represented as \(-1\).
The rounded coefficient is used as a Hessian lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f''(x)=-1-2^{-54}<-1=\widehat a\quad\text{and}\quad q(x)-f(x)=2^{-55}x^2>0\ \text{for }x\ne0.\)

notation.meaning: Quadratic model formed from the rounded estimate.

knowledge_statements.title: Nearest Rounding Can Reverse a Curvature Lower Bound

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on a box \(X\).
Curvature bounds are computed using finite-precision interval data.
A lower bound is called rigorous only when all enclosures use directed outward rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A curvature certificate is valid only if the computed interval Hessian contains every \(\nabla^2f(x)\) and its verified spectral bound does not exceed their least eigenvalues.

notation.meaning: Computed interval enclosure of the Hessian range.

review_flags: A dedicated validated-numerics source for Hessian enclosures is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification boundary between rounded curvature estimates and validated Hessian bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\boldsymbol H(X)\) be a computed interval matrix intended to enclose \(\{\nabla^2f(x):x\in X\}\). A rigorous curvature lower bound \(\underline\lambda\) requires both \[\nabla^2f(x)\in\boldsymbol H(X)\quad\text{for every }x\in X\] and a verified conclusion \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\ge\underline\lambda\) for every \(H\in\boldsymbol H(X)\). Nearest-rounded evaluation can exclude attainable Hessian entries or overestimate \(\underline\lambda\); either event invalidates any underestimator whose correctness depends on that curvature bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-precision curvature estimates certify bounds only when outward-rounded interval Hessians enclose every true Hessian and the spectral lower bound is itself verified.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Curvature Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certification conditions are plausible and fit the failure-boundary leaf, but the finite-precision and verified spectral-enclosure claims require a specific validated-numerics source.

children.title: Numerical versus Rigorous Bounds
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for finite-precision estimates that do not constitute validated certificates.

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the feasible set of a minimization problem.
All computations used for certification account for rounding and expression domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reported value \(L\) is rigorous exactly when a validated argument establishes \(L\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\); numerical evidence alone does not establish this predicate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound distinction for finite-precision global minimization.

source_refs.locator: 3.6 Finite epsilon-Convergence and epsilon-Global Optimality p. 87
2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the minimization value \(f^*=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), a rigorous lower bound is a number \(L\) accompanied by a validated argument that \[L\le f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in F.\] The validation must include rounding-error control and correct handling of all expression domains used in deriving \(L\). A numerical lower-bound estimate is a floating-point value suggested by an algorithm but lacking that universal validated inequality. Numerical agreement, solver termination, or small residuals alone do not convert such an estimate into a rigorous bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rigorous lower bound comes with a validated universal inequality over the feasible set. A floating-point estimate, small residual, or solver termination alone is only numerical evidence.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical versus Rigorous Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 3.6 Finite epsilon-Convergence and epsilon-Global Optimality p. 87
2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This node is explicitly a navigation topic for organizing finite-precision estimates, not a terminal definition container. A standalone definition record therefore does not fit its immutable role.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Numerical Objective Value Is Not a Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed example contrasting a feasible objective value with a minimization lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{x\in[-1,1]}x^2\), a feasible point \(\hat x=10^{-6}\) has value \(10^{-12}\), which is an upper bound rather than a lower bound on the optimum \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small feasible objective value is an upper bound, not a minimization lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\hat x)=10^{-12}>f^*=0\), so it is not a lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: A Numerical Objective Value Is Not a Lower Bound

intermediate_metadata.reason: Publication is deferred because the immutable role makes this a navigation container and neither the deferred definition nor the proposed feasible-point example resolves its terminal content contract. Relaxation weakness and curvature-bound reliability remain excluded to siblings; positive validation machinery remains in method-specific certificate leaves.

children.title: Model-Domain Regularity Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by singular expressions, degenerate feasible geometry, or inaccurate analytic information.

children.title: Expression-Domain Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for poles and domain-restricted elementary operations.

children.title: Singular Expressions
children.top_down_role: Expressions exhibiting poles or unbounded local behavior within relevant domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Expressions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of ordinary connected interval reciprocal evaluation when a denominator enclosure contains zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a box, let \(g:X\to\mathbb R\), and suppose an expression contains \(1/g(x)\). If an inclusion interval extension satisfies \(g(X)\subseteq G(X)\) and \(0\in G(X)\), ordinary connected interval arithmetic cannot assign a finite interval enclosure to \(1/G(X)\). A finite reciprocal bound can be certified only after additional domain reasoning, subdivision, or a strengthened enclosure excludes zero from the denominator range on the region being certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an interval enclosure of a denominator contains zero, ordinary connected interval reciprocal evaluation cannot produce a finite certified enclosure. Additional domain reasoning, subdivision, or a stronger enclosure must exclude zero first.
assumptions_latex: An inclusion interval extension satisfies \(g(X)\subseteq G(X)\) and \(0\in G(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1/G(X)\) has no finite connected interval enclosure under ordinary interval division; certification of a finite reciprocal bound requires excluding zero from the denominator range on the certified region.

notation.meaning: Interval enclosure of the denominator range.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation-from-zero condition sufficient for a finite connected reciprocal enclosure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(X)=[\underline g,\overline g]\) enclose \(g(X)\). If \(\underline g>0\), then \(1/g(X)\subseteq[1/\overline g,1/\underline g]\). If \(\overline g<0\), then \(1/g(X)\subseteq[1/\underline g,1/\overline g]\). In either case, \(\inf_{x\in X}|g(x)|\ge\operatorname{dist}(0,G(X))>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Excluding zero from a denominator enclosure certifies domain validity and a finite reciprocal bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in X}|g(x)|\ge\operatorname{dist}(0,G(X))>0.

notation.meaning: Certified separation of the denominator enclosure from zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Reciprocal-Bound Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interval Inclusion of Zero Is Not a Singularity Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependency counterexample separating interval-evaluation failure from an actual denominator zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=[0,1]\), let \(g(x)=x-x+1\), so \(g(x)=1\) for every \(x\in X\). Natural interval evaluation gives \(G(X)=[0,1]-[0,1]+1=[0,2]\), which contains zero. Thus ordinary connected interval reciprocal evaluation is unresolved even though \(1/g(x)=1\) is defined and bounded throughout \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval dependency can place zero in a denominator enclosure even when the actual denominator is identically nonzero.
assumptions_latex: Natural interval evaluation treats the repeated occurrences of \(x\) independently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in G(X)\quad\text{but}\quad 0\notin g(X)=\{1\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval Inclusion of Zero Is Not a Singularity Certificate

children.title: Undefined Elementary Operations
children.top_down_role: Elementary operations whose admissible domains exclude part of a search region.

knowledge_statements.title: Undefined Elementary Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a real-valued expression outside the joint domains of its elementary operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an expression tree define a nominal objective or constraint \(e:X\rightharpoonup\mathbb R\). Its effective domain \(D_e\subseteq X\) consists of points at which every node is defined recursively; in particular, a denominator must be nonzero, a real logarithm argument positive, and a real even-root argument nonnegative. If the search region \(B\subseteq X\) is not contained in \(D_e\), then \(e\) is not a real-valued function on all of \(B\). Consequently, any global-optimization formulation or bound requiring finite real values throughout \(B\) is invalid unless it restricts the domain, partitions away invalid points, or adopts an explicit extended-value convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expression is not a real-valued model on a search region containing division by zero, invalid logarithms, or invalid roots unless those points are excluded or assigned explicit extended values.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the nominal model domain.
Elementary operations are interpreted over the real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\nsubseteq D_e\Longrightarrow e\text{ is not real-valued on all of }B\).

notation.meaning: Effective real domain of the expression tree.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 General Problem Statement and Special Model Forms p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 General Problem Statement and Special Model Forms p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimization encoding of an expression's effective-domain restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e:D_e\to\mathbb R\), let \(X\cap D_e\ne\varnothing\), and define \(\bar e(x)=e(x)\) for \(x\in D_e\) and \(\bar e(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then \(\inf_{x\in X}\bar e(x)=\inf_{x\in X\cap D_e}e(x)\), and their minimizer sets coincide. This convention does not make the original elementary expression real-valued outside \(D_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning positive infinity outside an expression's effective domain exactly encodes domain restriction for minimization.
assumptions_latex: The model is a minimization problem.
Undefined points are assigned \(+\infty\), not an arbitrary finite value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in X}\bar e(x)=\inf_{x\in X\cap D_e}e(x),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\bar e(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X\cap D_e}e(x).

notation.meaning: Extended-real domain-restricting version of the expression.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Value Domain Encoding

children.title: Pole-Proximal Regions
children.top_down_role: Search regions near singularities where bounds or evaluations become unstable.

knowledge_statements.title: Pole-Proximal Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhoods in which a denominator approaches a zero producing a pole or unbounded variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p,q:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and let \(r(x)=p(x)/q(x)\) wherever \(q(x)\ne0\). For \(\delta>0\), the pole-proximal region is \(P_\delta=\{x\in X:0<|q(x)|\le\delta\}\). If \(x_k\in P_\delta\), \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(q(\bar x)=0\), and \(|p(x_k)|\ge c>0\), then \(|r(x_k)|\to\infty\). Thus boxes intersecting arbitrarily small \(P_\delta\) generally admit no finite range bound for \(r\) without separating the zero set of \(q\) or proving cancellation by \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pole-proximal region contains points with a small nonzero denominator. Near an uncancelled denominator zero, the quotient becomes unbounded and finite box bounds fail.
assumptions_latex: The numerator remains bounded away from zero along the stated sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|r(x_k)|\to\infty\) as \(q(x_k)\to0\) under noncancellation.

notation.meaning: Region where the denominator is nonzero but at most delta in magnitude.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cancellation condition distinguishing a genuine pole from a represented denominator zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that on a punctured neighborhood of \(\bar x\), \(p(x)=q(x)h(x)\), where \(h\) is continuous at \(\bar x\). Then \(p(x)/q(x)=h(x)\) wherever \(q(x)\ne0\), and the quotient has the finite removable extension \(r(\bar x)=h(\bar x)\). Thus a denominator zero alone does not imply pole-proximal blow-up.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common factor can make an apparent denominator zero removable, so proximity to a represented zero is not by itself proof of a pole.
assumptions_latex: \(p=qh\) on a punctured neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{x\to\bar x,\ q(x)\ne0}\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}=h(\bar x).
knowledge_statements.title: Removable-Singularity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit magnitude bound for a quotient near a denominator zero without cancellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=p/q\) on a region \(R\) where \(|p(x)|\ge c>0\) and \(0<|q(x)|\le\delta\). Then \(|r(x)|\ge c/\delta\) for every \(x\in R\). Consequently, for a family of such regions with fixed \(c>0\) and \(\delta\downarrow0\), the quotient magnitude diverges uniformly at least on the scale \(c/\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without cancellation, quotient magnitudes grow at least inversely with the denominator scale in a pole-proximal region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in R}\left|\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right|\ge\frac{c}{\delta}.

notation.meaning: Certified inverse-denominator scale for quotient magnitude.

knowledge_statements.title: Quantitative Pole-Proximity Growth

children.title: Domain-Violation Detection
children.top_down_role: Identification and localization of invalid expression domains during search.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Violation Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound interval certificates for excluding boxes on which an elementary operation is nowhere defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a box, let \(a(B)\) be an inclusion interval satisfying \(a(x)\in a(B)\) for every \(x\in B\), and let \(D_\phi\subseteq\mathbb R\) be the real domain of an elementary operation \(\phi\). The condition \(a(B)\cap D_\phi=\varnothing\) certifies that \(\phi(a(x))\) is undefined for every \(x\in B\), so \(B\) may be rejected. If \(a(B)\) intersects both \(D_\phi\) and its complement, interval evaluation alone is inconclusive: the box must be subdivided or analyzed with a sharper domain test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inclusion interval disjoint from an operation's real domain certifies that an entire box is invalid. A mixed interval does not certify validity or invalidity.
assumptions_latex: \(D_\phi\) is the exact real domain of \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a(B)\cap D_\phi=\varnothing\Longrightarrow B\cap\operatorname{dom}(\phi\circ a)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Inclusion interval for the argument expression over the box.
Real scalar domain of the elementary operation.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nodewise procedure for classifying boxes as invalid, valid, or unresolved for a factorable expression graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Process a finite acyclic expression graph in topological order using inclusion enclosures. At a node \(v=\phi(a)\), reject \(B\) if \(a(B)\cap D_\phi=\varnothing\), certify that node as domain-valid if \(a(B)\subseteq D_\phi\), and otherwise mark the node unresolved. Certify the entire expression as domain-valid only when every node is certified valid; sharpen or subdivide unresolved boxes rather than rejecting them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain screening propagates enclosures through the expression graph, rejecting only certified-invalid boxes and retaining mixed cases for refinement.
assumptions_latex: Every propagated enclosure contains the corresponding node range.
The expression graph is finite and acyclic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Every rejected box is disjoint from the effective domain of the expression.}

notation.meaning: An elementary operation node and its argument expression.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Expression-Graph Domain Screening

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary inclusion certificate proving that an elementary operation is defined throughout a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(a(B)\) encloses \(a(x)\) for every \(x\in B\) and \(a(B)\subseteq D_\phi\), then \(\phi(a(x))\) is defined for every \(x\in B\). For \(D_{\log}=(0,\infty)\), a closed interval enclosure therefore needs a strictly positive lower endpoint to certify whole-box validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An argument enclosure contained in an operation's exact real domain certifies validity everywhere on the box.
assumptions_latex: \(D_\phi\) is the exact real domain of \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a(B)\subseteq D_\phi\Longrightarrow B\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\phi\circ a).
knowledge_statements.title: Whole-Box Domain-Validity Certificate

children.title: Discontinuity-Induced Regularity Failures
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for reformulations that destroy continuity or usable regularity.

children.title: Discontinuous Model Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extensions outside natural domains that introduce discontinuities into a model.

knowledge_statements.title: Discontinuous Model Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of continuity when a partial or restricted model is extended by incompatible exterior values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and define an extension \(F:X\to\mathbb R\) by \(F(x)=f(x)\) for \(x\in D\) and \(F(x)=g(x)\) for \(x\notin D\). At a boundary point \(\bar x\in\partial D\), continuity of \(F\) requires every interior and exterior sequence converging to \(\bar x\) to have the common limit \(F(\bar x)\). If the corresponding limits of \(f\) and \(g\) exist but differ, then \(F\) is discontinuous at \(\bar x\), even when both pieces are continuous on their respective domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pasting continuous model pieces does not preserve continuity when their limiting values disagree at the interface.
assumptions_latex: The one-sided sequential limits of the two pieces exist at the boundary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\lim_{D
i x	o ar x}f(x)
e\lim_{X\setminus D
i x	o ar x}g(x)\Longrightarrow F	ext{ is discontinuous at } ar x\).

notation.meaning: Boundary of the original model domain.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Formulation of the Global Optimization Problem p. 6

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Formulation of the Global Optimization Problem p. 6

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided lower-semicontinuity condition for an extension across a relatively closed model domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be closed relative to \(X\), let \(F=f\) on \(D\) and \(F=g\) on \(X\setminus D\), and assume that \(f\) and \(g\) are lower semicontinuous on their relative domains. Then \(F\) is lower semicontinuous on \(X\) if and only if \(f(\bar x)\le \liminf_{X\setminus D\ni x\to\bar x}g(x)\) for every \(\bar x\in\partial_XD\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed-domain extension remains lower semicontinuous exactly when exterior limiting values never fall below the assigned boundary value.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are lower semicontinuous on their relative domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is lower semicontinuous on }X\iff f(\bar x)\le\liminf_{X\setminus D\ni x\to\bar x}g(x)\quad\forall\bar x\in\partial_XD.

notation.meaning: Boundary of the original domain relative to X.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuous Exterior Extension Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient continuity condition for a two-piece extension at its interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f\) on \(D\subseteq X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(F=g\) on \(X\setminus D\), and let \(\bar x\in\partial_XD\). Then \(F\) is continuous at \(\bar x\) if and only if \(f(x_k)\to F(\bar x)\) for every sequence \(x_k\in D\) converging to \(\bar x\), and \(g(y_k)\to F(\bar x)\) for every sequence \(y_k\in X\setminus D\) converging to \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise extension is continuous at an interface exactly when both one-sided sequential limits equal its assigned boundary value.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is defined by the stated two pieces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is continuous at }\bar x\iff \lim_{D\ni x\to\bar x}f(x)=F(\bar x)=\lim_{X\setminus D\ni x\to\bar x}g(x).

notation.meaning: Boundary of D relative to X.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Boundary Compatibility Criterion

children.title: Discontinuous Penalty Constructions
children.top_down_role: Penalty representations whose transitions destroy continuity.

knowledge_statements.title: Discontinuous Penalty Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicator penalties that encode feasibility but introduce a jump at the feasible boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(C\subset X\) be closed with nonempty boundary, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and choose \(M>0\). Define \(F_M(x)=f(x)+M\mathbf 1_{X\setminus C}(x)\). For any \(\bar x\in\partial C\) and sequences \(x_k\in C\), \(y_k\in X\setminus C\) converging to \(\bar x\), continuity of \(f\) gives \(F_M(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\) and \(F_M(y_k)\to f(\bar x)+M\). Hence the constant exterior penalty creates a jump of size \(M\) at every two-sided boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a fixed cost to every infeasible point creates a boundary jump, even when the original objective is continuous and the feasible set is closed.
assumptions_latex: Both feasible and infeasible sequences approach the selected boundary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_M\text{ is discontinuous at every such }\bar x\in\partial C\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1 General Problem Statement and Special Model Forms p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 General Problem Statement and Special Model Forms p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exactness Condition for a Fixed Exterior Penalty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise condition under which the penalized problem has exactly the constrained minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\), suppose \(v_C=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) is attained, and define \(F_M=f\) on \(C\) and \(F_M=f+M\) on \(X\setminus C\). Then \(\operatorname*{argmin}_XF_M=\operatorname*{argmin}_Cf\) if and only if \(f(x)+M>v_C\) for every \(x\in X\setminus C\). The stronger uniform separation \(\inf_{X\setminus C}(f+M)>v_C\) is sufficient but is not necessary when the exterior infimum equals \(v_C\) without being attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed exterior penalty preserves exactly the constrained minimizers when every infeasible penalized value is strictly above the constrained optimum.
assumptions_latex: The penalty equals the constant \(M\) at every infeasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{X}F_M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{C}f\iff \forall x\in X\setminus C,\ f(x)+M>v_C.

notation.meaning: Optimal objective value on the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Condition for a Fixed Exterior Penalty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semicontinuity of a Fixed Exterior Penalty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided regularity retained by a positive indicator penalty on a closed feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\) be relatively closed, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and define \(F_M=f+M\mathbf 1_{X\setminus C}\) with \(M>0\). Then \(F_M\) is lower semicontinuous on \(X\). At every \(\bar x\in\partial_XC\) approachable from \(X\setminus C\), \(F_M\) is not upper semicontinuous and therefore is not continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive fixed exterior penalty over a closed feasible set is lower semicontinuous but jumps upward outside the feasible boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_M\text{ is lower semicontinuous on }X\text{ and is not upper semicontinuous at each two-sided boundary point.}

notation.meaning: Objective with a fixed exterior indicator penalty.

knowledge_statements.title: Semicontinuity of a Fixed Exterior Penalty

children.title: Regularity Loss
children.top_down_role: Loss of exploitable continuity, smoothness, or modulus information after reformulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A persistent jump excludes continuity, local Lipschitz continuity, and differentiability at an interior point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(F:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\bar x\in X\). Suppose there are sequences \(x_k,y_k\in X\) converging to \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\eta>0\) such that \(|F(x_k)-F(y_k)|\ge\eta\) for every \(k\). Then \(F\) is not continuous at \(\bar x\). Moreover, no neighborhood \(U\subseteq X\) of \(\bar x\) admits a finite constant \(L\) satisfying \(|F(x)-F(y)|\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in U\), because \(\|x_k-y_k\|\to0\) while the value gap remains positive. Consequently, \(F\) is not differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior point, a persistent positive value gap between pairs of convergent sequences destroys continuity, local Lipschitz continuity, and differentiability.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(\bar x\in X\).
Both sequences converge to \(\bar x\) and retain a uniform positive value gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is neither continuous nor locally Lipschitz nor differentiable at }\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Uniform positive lower bound on the value gap.

source_refs.locator: Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case p. 39

source_witnesses.locator: Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case p. 39

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Attainment without Lower Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-domain example of an optimization consequence that can accompany discontinuity-induced regularity loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) by \(F(0)=1\) and \(F(x)=x\) for \(x>0\). Then \(\inf_{[0,1]}F=0\), but no point attains the infimum. Moreover, \(F(0)>\liminf_{x\to0}F(x)=0\), so \(F\) is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness alone does not ensure attainment after lower semicontinuity is lost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in[0,1]}F(x)=0\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname*{argmin}_{[0,1]}F=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Attainment without Lower Semicontinuity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Every Vanishing Continuity Modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strengthens the seed from Lipschitz failure to failure of every local modulus tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the assumptions of the immutable seed, let \(\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) satisfy \(\omega(t)\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\). No neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) can satisfy \(|F(x)-F(y)|\le\omega(\|x-y\|)\) for all \(x,y\in U\). In particular, the jump excludes every local Hölder estimate as well as local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A persistent jump defeats every local continuity modulus that vanishes with distance, including all Hölder and Lipschitz bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists U\ni\bar x:\ |F(x)-F(y)|\le\omega(\|x-y\|)\quad\forall x,y\in U.

notation.meaning: A candidate continuity modulus vanishing at zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Every Vanishing Continuity Modulus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General extended-real compact-attainment theorem proposed by the Builder.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is nonempty and compact and \(F:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, then \(F\) attains its minimum on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous function attains its minimum on a nonempty compact domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x)\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Attainment under Lower Semicontinuity

intermediate_metadata.reason: The local inventory covers the hierarchy of regularity destroyed by a persistent jump and a compact-domain nonattainment example when lower semicontinuity is lost. The general compact-attainment theorem is deferred to its canonical home; concrete extension, penalty, and boundary-artifact mechanisms remain sibling-owned.

children.title: Boundary-Artifact Regimes
children.top_down_role: Artificial behavior introduced near extension or penalty boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Artifact Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Artificial cliffs created solely by a discontinuous extension at a model-domain boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[-1,1]\), let \(C=[0,1]\), and let the original objective be \(f(x)=x\) on \(C\). Extend it to \(X\) by \(F_M(x)=x+M\mathbf 1_{[-1,0)}(x)\), where \(M>1\). The original constrained problem has minimum \(f(0)=0\). However, \(F_M\) has a jump at zero, with \(\lim_{x\uparrow0}F_M(x)=M\) and \(\lim_{x\downarrow0}F_M(x)=0\). Thus the extended landscape contains an artificial cliff of size \(M\) at the feasible boundary that is absent from the continuous objective on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed infeasibility penalty can create an artificial cliff at the feasible boundary even though the original constrained objective is continuous there.
assumptions_latex: The exterior value is imposed by the stated indicator extension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_M\text{ has a boundary jump of size }M\text{ at }0\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Formulation of the Global Optimization Problem p. 6

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Formulation of the Global Optimization Problem p. 6

children.title: Feasible-Geometry Degeneracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for equality-dominated and ill-conditioned feasible geometry.

children.title: Thin Feasible Regions
children.top_down_role: Feasible sets occupying very small volume within the surrounding search domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Thin Feasible Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible sets whose ambient thickness is zero or uniformly small relative to the search scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). The feasible region is ambiently thin if \(C\) has empty interior in \(X\); equivalently, no relative open ball of positive radius is contained in \(C\). A quantitative \(\varepsilon\)-thin regime occurs when the inradius \(\rho(C;X)=\sup\{r\ge0:\exists x\in C,\ B(x,r)\cap X\subseteq C\}\) satisfies \(\rho(C;X)\le\varepsilon\). Empty-interior sets have \(\rho(C;X)=0\), while narrow full-dimensional corridors may have positive but small inradius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible region is thin when it contains no ambient open ball, or quantitatively when its largest contained ball is small relative to the search scale.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) carries the relative Euclidean topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_X(C)=\varnothing\Longrightarrow\rho(C;X)=0\).

notation.meaning: Relative inradius of the feasible set.
Euclidean ball of center x and radius r.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topological Thinness Does Not Imply Small Volume
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating empty interior from measure-zero or low-volume feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a compact set \(C\subset[0,1]\) with empty relative interior and positive Lebesgue measure. In particular, the Smith--Volterra--Cantor set satisfies \(\operatorname{int}_{[0,1]}(C)=\varnothing\) and \(\lambda_1(C)=\tfrac12\). Thus empty relative interior, equivalently zero relative inradius for this compact set, does not imply zero ambient measure or zero probability under every absolutely continuous sampling law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible set may have empty interior and zero inradius while retaining positive volume; the Smith–Volterra–Cantor set is a standard example.
assumptions_latex: Thinness is interpreted as empty relative interior in \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_{[0,1]}(C)=\varnothing\not\Longrightarrow\lambda_1(C)=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Topological Thinness Does Not Imply Small Volume

children.title: Degenerate Feasible Geometry
children.top_down_role: Feasible-set geometry lacking robust local dimension or conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Feasible Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local constraint geometry with dependent active gradients and failure of the linear independence constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m;\ h_j(x)=0,\ j=1,\ldots,p\}\), where all constraint functions are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\in C\). Let \(I(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\). The feasible geometry is LICQ-degenerate at \(\bar x\) when the family \(\{\nabla g_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}\cup\{\nabla h_j(\bar x):j=1,\ldots,p\}\) is linearly dependent. This includes redundant active constraints and vanishing active gradients. In this regime, LICQ-based existence or uniqueness guarantees for local multiplier representations are unavailable, although a particular problem may still have unique multipliers for other reasons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible geometry is LICQ-degenerate when the gradients of active inequalities and equalities are linearly dependent at a feasible point; consequently, LICQ-based multiplier guarantees do not apply.
assumptions_latex: All constraint functions are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}\{\nabla g_i(\bar x),\nabla h_j(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x),\ 1\le j\le p\}<|I(\bar x)|+p\).

notation.meaning: Index set of active inequality constraints.
Feasible set defined by smooth equalities and inequalities.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weaker smooth constraint-qualification boundary and its abnormal-multiplier alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a feasible point \( ar x\), MFCQ holds when the equality gradients are linearly independent and there exists \(d\) satisfying \(
abla h_j( ar x)^Td=0\) for every equality and \(
abla g_i( ar x)^Td<0\) for every active inequality. LICQ implies MFCQ, but not conversely. MFCQ fails if and only if there is a nonzero pair \((\lambda,\mu)\), with \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for active inequalities, such that \(\sum_{i\in I( ar x)}\lambda_i
abla g_i( ar x)+\sum_j\mu_j
abla h_j( ar x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MFCQ fails exactly when the active constraint gradients admit a nonzero abnormal dependence with nonnegative inequality coefficients.
assumptions_latex: All constraints are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
eg\mathrm{MFCQ}( ar x)\iff\exists(\lambda,\mu)
e0:\ \lambda\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I( ar x)}\lambda_i
abla g_i( ar x)+\sum_j\mu_j
abla h_j( ar x)=0.

notation.meaning: A strict feasible direction for the active linearized inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Mangasarian–Fromovitz Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent descriptions of one feasible set can have different active-gradient degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C=\{0\}\subset\mathbb R\) is represented both by \(h_1(x)=x=0\), whose gradient at zero is nonzero, and by \(h_2(x)=x^2=0\), whose gradient at zero vanishes. Thus LICQ degeneracy is a property of the chosen constraint representation at the point, not solely of the underlying feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent equality descriptions of the same feasible set can differ in whether their active gradients are degenerate.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Dependence of Gradient Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT Failure under a Vanishing Active Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal example showing failure of KKT necessity under degenerate constraint geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x\) subject to \(x^2\le0\). The sole feasible point \(x=0\) is the global minimizer, but the active constraint gradient is zero. The KKT stationarity equation \(1+\lambda(2x)=0\) therefore reduces to \(1=0\) at \(x=0\), so no multiplier \(\lambda\ge0\) exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global minimizer can fail the KKT equations when its active constraint has a vanishing gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*=0\text{ is globally optimal, but no }\lambda\ge0\text{ satisfies KKT stationarity.}
knowledge_statements.title: KKT Failure under a Vanishing Active Gradient

children.title: Equality-Dominated Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Models whose feasible sets are largely determined by equality constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Dominated Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility confined locally to lower-dimensional equality sets in the ambient search space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\) be continuously differentiable, let \(g:X\to\mathbb R^m\), and define \(C=\{x\in X:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Feasibility is equality-dominated near \(\bar x\in C\) if \(p\ge1\) and \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=p\) throughout a neighborhood of \(\bar x\). Then \(h^{-1}(0)\) is locally an \((n-p)\)-dimensional embedded manifold, and \(C\), being locally contained in this manifold, has zero \(n\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure near \(\bar x\). Thus exact feasible points occupy no positive-volume subset of a sufficiently small ambient neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locally independent equality constraints confine nearby feasible points to a lower-dimensional manifold, so exact feasibility has zero ambient volume near the point.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\) is continuously differentiable.
\(p\ge1\), \(\bar x\in C\), and \(Dh\) has full row rank \(p\) near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is locally contained in an }(n-p)\text{-dimensional manifold and has local }n\text{-dimensional measure }0\).

notation.meaning: Number of locally independent equality constraints.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.1 Elementary algebraic geometry p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Probability of Exact Equality Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampling consequence of regular equality-defined feasibility having zero ambient measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(h\in C^1(U;\mathbb R^p)\) with \(p\ge1\), and suppose \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=p\) for every \(x\in h^{-1}(0)\). If the law of a random vector \(Z\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(n\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure, then \(\mathbb P(Z\in C)=0\) for every measurable \(C\subseteq h^{-1}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ambient sample with an absolutely continuous distribution hits a regular positive-codimension equality-feasible set with probability zero.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(h\in C^1(U;\mathbb R^p)\).
\(p\ge1\) and \(Dh\) has full row rank on \(h^{-1}(0)\).
\(C\subseteq h^{-1}(0)\) is measurable and the law of \(Z\) is absolutely continuous with respect to ambient Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(Z\in C)=0\).

notation.meaning: Random point sampled in the ambient space.
Measurable feasible set contained in the equality zero set.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Probability of Exact Equality Feasibility

children.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of apparent feasibility on numerical acceptance tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric and sampling sensitivity caused by replacing an exact equality with a residual-tolerance band.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X=[-1,1]^n\), let \(h:X\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(h(x)=x_1\), and define \(C_\tau=\{x\in X:|h(x)|\le\tau\}\) for \(\tau\ge0\). Then \(C_0=\{x\in X:x_1=0\}\) has zero \(n\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure. For \(0<\tau\le1\), one has \(C_\tau=[-\tau,\tau]\times[-1,1]^{n-1}\) and \(\lambda_n(C_\tau)=2^n\tau\). Thus every positive tolerance changes the exact zero-volume set into a positive-volume band. Under uniform sampling on \(X\), the probability of tolerance-feasibility is \(\lambda_n(C_\tau)/\lambda_n(X)=\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In this equality example, any positive residual tolerance turns a zero-volume feasible set into a band whose volume, and whose acceptance probability under uniform sampling, grows linearly with the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility uses the absolute residual tolerance \(\tau\).
The acceptance-probability statement uses uniform sampling on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_n(C_0)=0\), while \(\lambda_n(C_\tau)=2^n\tau>0\) and \(\mathbb P(X_{\mathrm{unif}}\in C_\tau)=\tau\) for \(0<\tau\le1\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set under residual tolerance tau.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.2 Solvability of the Global Optimization Problem p. 4

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.2 Solvability of the Global Optimization Problem p. 4

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set and optimal-value limits for residual tolerances on a compact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a compact metric space, let \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\) be continuous, and define \(C_\tau=\{x\in X:\|h(x)\|\le\tau\}\). Then \(C_{\tau_1}\subseteq C_{\tau_2}\) for \(0\le\tau_1\le\tau_2\), and \(C_0=\bigcap_{\tau>0}C_\tau\). If \(\tau_k\downarrow0\) and \(x_k\in C_{\tau_k}\), every cluster point of \((x_k)\) belongs to \(C_0\). If additionally \(C_0\ne\varnothing\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, then \(v(\tau)=\min_{x\in C_\tau}f(x)\) increases to \(v(0)\) as \(\tau\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact domain with continuous residuals, tolerance-feasible sets shrink to the exact feasible set, and their minimum values converge monotonically to the exact constrained value.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a compact metric space and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\) is continuous.
For the value statement, \(C_0\ne\varnothing\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_0=\bigcap_{\tau>0}C_\tau,\quad x_k\in C_{\tau_k},\ \tau_k\downarrow0\Longrightarrow \operatorname{cluster}(x_k)\subseteq C_0,\quad \lim_{\tau\downarrow0}v(\tau)=v(0).

notation.meaning: Feasible set under residual tolerance tau.
Minimum objective value over the tolerance-feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Tolerance Set and Value Convergence

children.title: Unknown or Misspecified Modulus Information
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for missing, nonconservative, or excessively conservative variation estimates.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown or Misspecified Modulus Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure modes caused by absent, underestimated, or excessively conservative variation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le L_*\|x-y\|\) on \(X\), with true minimal Lipschitz modulus \(L_*\). A global method using an estimate \(\widehat L\) has three regimes: if no finite \(\widehat L\) is available, Lipschitz lower bounds cannot be instantiated; if \(\widehat L<L_*\), the bound \(f(x)\ge f(y)-\widehat L\|x-y\|\) need not hold and pruning may discard a global minimizer; if \(\widehat L\ge L_*\), bounds are valid, but excessive overestimation weakens them and can severely enlarge the required partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Missing modulus information prevents Lipschitz bounds; underestimation makes pruning unsound; overestimation remains valid but can make global search inefficient.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(f\) has finite true Lipschitz modulus \(L_*\).
The method constructs lower bounds using \(\widehat L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat L<L_*\) may invalidate bounds, whereas \(\widehat L\ge L_*\) preserves validity but may reduce sharpness.

notation.meaning: Minimal valid Lipschitz modulus of the objective.
Modulus estimate used by the optimization method.
